project.name: chang-store
project.description: AI-powered virtual fashion studio built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. It enables users to generate fashion imagery including virtual try-ons, lookbooks, background swaps, pose changes, and more using Google Gemini, Grok (xAI), and GPT Image (OpenAI). Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to understand what chang-store is trying to do before reading implementation details. It frames the app as an AI-powered virtual fashion studio, introduces the Gemini-first architecture, and explains the parallel Grok and GPT Image provider studios. This gives you the product story and the high-level Component → Hook → Service → API mental model that the rest of the tour will keep unpacking.

tour.title: Bootstrap Entry
tour.description: The runtime story begins in index.tsx, the code entry point identified by the graph traversal. Its job is intentionally small: mount the React tree and hand control to the main app shell. This is the cleanest place to see where the browser lifecycle starts and how little logic is allowed at the edge.
tour.languageLesson: In React + Vite apps, the entry file is usually a tiny bootstrap module that creates the root and renders the top-level component. Keeping bootstrap code thin makes application startup easier to reason about and test.

tour.title: App Shell
tour.description: App.tsx is the central coordinator of the studio and sits at depth 1 in the BFS traversal, so it is the natural next stop after bootstrap. It switches between features, arranges the main layout, and wires together the major providers and global UI surfaces. Read it alongside types.ts, the most depended-on file in the graph, because the app shell is largely driven by shared enums and cross-cutting domain types defined there.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript shared type modules often become high fan-in files because they define the vocabulary the whole app speaks. When a types file is this central, it usually marks the boundary between product concepts and implementation details.

tour.title: Global Context Layer
tour.description: Once you understand the shell, study the contexts that carry global state through the app. LanguageContext establishes translation and locale behavior, ApiProviderContext supplies provider selection and API wiring, and ImageGalleryContext manages the cross-feature image collection. Together they explain how the app avoids prop drilling and why many feature screens can stay thin while still sharing stateful capabilities.
tour.languageLesson: React Context is best for truly global concerns such as language, provider configuration, and shared galleries. A good teaching pattern here is to distinguish context state from feature-local hook state: context is ambient infrastructure, while hooks encapsulate workflow logic.

tour.title: Model And Provider Catalogs
tour.description: With the global state layer in mind, move to the registries that tell the app which models and providers exist. modelRegistry.ts describes capabilities and lookup rules for supported models, while providerRegistry.ts captures provider metadata, defaults, and environment-key resolution. These files matter because they turn product choices from Step 1 into configuration data that the UI and services can consume consistently.

tour.title: Gemini Service Facade
tour.description: The README narrative says Gemini workflows flow through a unified facade, and imageEditingService.ts is that boundary. It consolidates generation, editing, upscaling, and chat-oriented image workflows behind one service surface, which lets hooks stay focused on state and user interaction instead of API mechanics. By this point in the tour, you can see the architecture chain clearly: app shell selects a workflow, hooks manage state, and this facade executes the work.

tour.title: Provider Studios
tour.description: After the Gemini path, compare it with the isolated provider-studio path. The provider-studios.md document explains the contract for Gemini, Grok, and GPT Image studios, and gptImageService.ts shows what a provider-specific REST integration looks like in practice. This step is important because it teaches the repo's key architectural distinction: Gemini goes through a centralized facade, while provider studios have their own dedicated service boundary.
tour.languageLesson: When a codebase supports multiple AI providers, a registry-plus-adapter pattern keeps the UI stable while allowing each backend to have different request formats and capabilities. The document/code pairing here is especially valuable because the architectural rule is written down and then reflected in a concrete service implementation.

tour.title: Build And Runtime Config
tour.description: Now zoom out from application logic to the files that make the project runnable. package.json defines the development workflow, dependencies, and quality-gate commands, while .env.example documents the secrets and flags the app expects at runtime. This is where a newcomer learns how the codebase is built, tested, and configured without yet touching deployment infrastructure.
tour.languageLesson: In Vite-based frontends, environment configuration is not just about setting variables; it is also about understanding which variables are exposed to client code and how build tooling injects them. Template env files are a safe way to document required secrets without committing real credentials.

tour.title: Deployment Surface
tour.description: Finish with vercel.json to see how the finished frontend is delivered in production. This file captures hosting-specific behavior such as response headers, making it the last piece in the journey from source code to a running web app. Ending here closes the loop: you have gone from product overview, to runtime flow, to shared architecture, and finally to deployment.
tour.languageLesson: Deployment config files are small but high leverage. For frontend apps, headers and platform settings often encode important production assumptions such as caching, framing rules, or security posture.
